chapters.title: Prologue
paragraphs: [The background shows the front of the Castle of PENTHEUS, King of Thebes. To one side stands the sacred Tomb of Semele, a small enclosure overgrown with wild vines, with a cleft in its rocky floor from which steam or smoke now and then escapes. The God DIONYSUS is discovered alone.]

DIONYSUS. Behold, the Son of God has come to this land of Thebes — I, Dionysus, whom the brand of heaven's hot splendor lit into life when she who bore me, Cadmus' daughter Semele, died here. Changed in shape from God to man, I walk again by the streams of Dirce and look upon the shore of Ismenus. There by the castle wall I see her place, the Tomb of the Lightning's Bride, the wreckage of those smoldering chambers, and the great faint wreaths of fire that never die — for the hatred Hera bore Semele has not died either. Cadmus has done well: he keeps this ground apart in purity, his daughter's sanctuary inviolate, and I have set my green and clustered vines to robe it round. Far behind me lie the golden lands of Lydia and Phrygia; far away the wide hot plains where Persian sunbeams play, the war-strongholds of Bactria, the storm-beaten clime of the Mede, Araby the Blest, and all of Asia that lies along the salt sea in proud embattled cities, woven motley-wise of Hellene and Barbarian. And now I come to Hellas — having taught all the rest of the world my dances and my rites of mystery, to show myself before the eyes of men as God made manifest. And first of all the Hellene lands I have come to wake Thebes; to set her hands to clasp my wand, my ivied javelin, and to hang my wild fawn-skin across her shoulders. For they have scorned me, those who least should have — Semele's own sisters; they mocked my birth and refused to believe that Dionysus was sprung from divine seed. My mother sinned, they said; some mortal lay with her, and at Cadmus' urging she covered her human shame with the dread name of Zeus, and for this lie God consumed her in flame. So they boast — and therefore my rod has fallen first upon them, and stung them wild-eyed from their empty chambers; the bare mountainside is now their home, and all their hearts are flame. I have bound the harness of my rites upon their necks. With them, every woman of Thebes — from cottage and from hall — has been goaded out by my magic. There, with the old King's daughters, in a confused rout, they make their dwelling between the roofless rocks and the shadowy green pines. Thus shall this Thebes, however sorely it smarts, learn and not forget — until she begs to take her part in worshipping me. So I must speak it plain, to save my mother's name and to crown myself here as true God, born of Semele to Zeus. Now Cadmus has yielded up his throne and royal honors to his daughter's son, Pentheus, who has begun a war against my body — a war against God. He shuts me out from due drink-offering, and when men pray, he never names my name. Therefore on his own head, and on his people's, my power shall be shown. Then to another land, when all is well here, I must go onward, making my godhead's might clear. But should this Theban town try in wrath and battle to drag down my Maenads, I myself shall stand in their path, and lead a maddened army into war for me. For this I have veiled my godhead in the wan form of mortal things and walk the earth as Man. O daughters of Tmolus, scattered now across the wide world — O Lydian band, my chosen and my own, women I lifted up across the eastern deep to wander where I wander and to sleep where I sleep — rise up, and wake the old sweet sound, the clang that I and mystic Rhea found, the Timbrel of the Mountain! Gather all Thebes to your song around Pentheus' royal hall. I go to seek my new-made worshippers, to lead their dances up the pine-clad slopes of Cithaeron.

[As he departs, there comes stealing in from the left a band of fifteen Eastern Women, the light of sunrise streaming on their long white robes and ivy-bound hair. They wear fawn-skins over the robes, and some carry timbrels, others pipes and other instruments. Many bear the thyrsus, the sacred Wand made of reed ringed with ivy. They enter stealthily until they see the place is empty, and then begin their mystic song of worship.]

chapters.title: Parodos
paragraphs: CHORUS. From Asia, from the rising of the dawn, to Bromius we have come, ever glorying in his name. We labored for our Lord through many shapes; we toiled, but the toil itself is the prize. Mystery — we hail you by your name!

CHORUS. Who lingers on the road? Who watches us pass? Let him hide himself indoors and not be bold. Let the heart that defies us keep its silence; for today I sing for Dionysus the song that is appointed from the beginning.

CHORUS. Blessed in every way is the man who has drunk from the Living Fountain, whose life no folly stains, whose soul stands near to God; whose sins are lifted off him like a fallen pall as he worships on the Mountain, and where Cybele our Mother ordains, his foot has trodden. With ivy heavy on his head and his thyrsus tossed high, for our God he lifts the cry: "Up, O Bacchae, wife and maiden! Come, O Bacchae, come! Bring the Joy-Giver, God-seed of God the Sower; bring Bromius in his power from Phrygia's mountain dome — to street and town and tower, oh, bring Bromius home!" Once, lying in anguish for an unborn life she longed for, his mother was cast to earth like a dead thing, struck down by the Thunder; her heart died, dying, in the white heart of fire. Then Zeus, Lord of Wonder, devised new lairs of birth: he tore his own flesh open to hide him, and with clasps of bitter gold he enclosed a secret son, and the Queen at his side did not know. When the perfect hour came, a horned God was found, a God crowned with serpents — and for that, his maidens twine serpents around the wands they bear, and the songs of serpents sound through the mazes of their hair.

CHORUS. All hail, O Thebes, you nurse of Semele! Crown your towers with Semele's wild ivy; oh, burst into bloom of wreathing bryony, berries and leaves and flowers; lift up the dark divine wand, the oak-wand and the pine-wand, and put on your fawn-skin, fringed in purity with fleecy white, like ours. Cleanse yourself in the proud waving of the wands! Yes, every man shall dance with us and pray, when Bromius leads his companies hillward, ever hillward, to where they stay — the flock of the Believing, the women lifted from loom and weaving, borne away by the magic of his breath.

CHORUS. Hail to you, O Nurse of Zeus, O Cavernous Haunt where fierce arms once clanged to guard God's rare cradle, where for you of old some crested Corybant first woke in Cretan air the wild orb of our orgies, our Timbrel; and your gorges rang with this strain, blended with Phrygian chant and the sweet keen pipes. But the Timbrel was another's, and away to Mother Rhea it had to go; and from the Mother's holy singing the mad Satyrs carried it back to us, to blend in the dancing and the cheer of our third and perfect Year — and at the last, it serves Dionysus!

CHORUS. O the gladness, the gladness on the mountains, to swoon in the race run out, when the holy fawn-skin clings, and all else falls away — to the joy of the red quick fountains, the blood of the hill-goat torn, the glory of wild-beast ravenings, where the hilltops catch the day. To the Phrygian, Lydian mountains! Bromius leads the way!

CHORUS. Then the earth streams with milk, yes, streams with wine and the nectar of the bee, and through the air drifts the dim perfume of Syrian frankincense; and He, our leader, tosses from his thyrsus a torchlight high and higher, like a beacon-fire, to wake the faint and the wandering; and as he sings he sets them leaping, his hair rippling to the sky, and beneath the Maenad cry his proud voice rings out: "Come, O Bacchae, come!"

CHORUS. Hither, O fragrant of Tmolus the Golden! Come with the voice of timbrel and drum; let the cry of your joyance lift up and embolden the God of the joy-cry. O Bacchanals, come! With pealing of pipes and with Phrygian clamor, on, where the vision of holiness thrills, where the music climbs and the maddening glamor — with the wild White Maids, to the hills, to the hills! Then, like a colt running by a river beside its mother, when the heart in him sings, with keen limbs drawn and the fleet foot quivering — away the Bacchanal springs!
[Enter TIRESIAS. He is an old man and blind, leaning on a staff and moving with slow stateliness, though wearing the Ivy and the Bacchic fawn-skin.]

chapters.title: First Episode
paragraphs: [Enter TIRESIAS. He is an old man and blind, leaning on a staff and moving with slow stateliness, though wearing the Ivy and the Bacchic fawn-skin.]

TIRESIAS. Hello, who keeps the gate? — Go, summon me Cadmus, son of Agenor, who crossed the sea from Sidon and built up this Theban citadel. Go, whoever you are. Tell him Tiresias is asking for him. He will know my errand himself, and the compact, age with age, that I made with him — gray hair with snow-white hair — to deck the new God's thyrsus, to wear his fawn-skin, and to crown our brows with ivy.
[Enter CADMUS from the Castle. He is even older than TIRESIAS, and wears the same attire.]

CADMUS. True friend! I knew that voice of yours, flowing like mellow wisdom from a wise fountain. And here I am, prepared, dressed in all the gear and harness of this God. Are we not told that he is the very soul of the dead life of old that sprang from my own daughter? Then surely you and I must with all our strength of men exalt him. Where shall I stand, then, where shall I tread the dance and toss this bowed and hoary head? O friend, in you is wisdom; guide my gray and worn-out steps, worn-out Tiresias. — No, I am not weak.

[At the first movement of worship his manner begins to change; a mysterious strength and exaltation enter into him.] Surely this arm could strike the wild earth with its thyrsus, day and night, and never tire! Sweetly and forgetfully the dim years fall away from me!
TIRESIAS. As with you, so with me. I am light and young, and I will try the dancing and the song.
CADMUS. Quick then — our chariots to the mountain road.
TIRESIAS. No; to take horses would be to mistrust the God.
CADMUS. So be it. My old arm shall guide you there.
TIRESIAS. The God himself shall guide! Have no care for that.
CADMUS. And in all Thebes shall no man dance but us?
TIRESIAS. Yes — Thebes is blinded. You and I can see.
CADMUS. The waiting is wearisome; hold my hand, friend; so.
TIRESIAS. Here is mine. Linked together, let us go.
CADMUS. Shall we, things of dust, despise the gods' dark ways?

TIRESIAS. Or test our wits against Heaven's high mysteries? Not you and I! That sublime heritage our fathers left us — wisdom old as time — no word of man, however deep his thought, however won by subtlest toil, can ever bring to nothing. Yes, men will rail that I forget my years, dancing and wreathing my white hair with ivy. What of it? The God has given no rule about which men should dance, the young or the old; he asks his honors from all mortals together, no one set apart; and great he shall be! [CADMUS, after looking off toward the Mountain.] Tiresias, since you cannot read this sight, I must be seer for you. Here in haste comes Pentheus, son of Echion, whom I raised up to rule my people in my place. — He looks alarmed. Stand close, and let us mark what we hear.
[The two stand back, partially concealed, while there enters in hot haste PENTHEUS, followed by a bodyguard. He is speaking to the SOLDIER in command.]

PENTHEUS. I had scarcely crossed our borders when my ear caught this strange rumor, that our own wives, our own sisters, have fled their hearths for wild and secret rites; that they cluster high on the shadowy hills, with dance and prayer to adore this newly minted god, this Dionysus — whoever he is! And in their gatherings deep wine-jars stand, and one by one they steal off into solitude, now this woman, now that, where some lover lies in wait — not God! It is the flame of Bacchus, they say, that wraps them. Bacchus! No — it is Aphrodite that they pray to. All the women I have caught, my men hold bound and shackled in our dungeon. The rest, I will go hunt them down! I'll snare these birds of mine in iron nets and put a stop to their prayer and mountain song and rites of rascaldom! They tell me, too, that there has come a stranger, a charmer and a man of spells, from the Lydian seas — a head all gold and cloudy fragrances, a wine-red cheek, and eyes that hold the very light of Aphrodite. Day and livelong night he haunts the company of girls, dangling his cup of joy before each lip! Let me get a grip on him, just once, inside these walls — and that wand of his will quickly fall silent, and that drift of tossing curls will lie still, when my rude sword falls between neck and trunk! It is all his story, this tale of Dionysus: how the same babe that was blasted with his dead mother by the lightning flame, on account of the mother's lie, was reconceived and born perfect from the thigh of Zeus, and is now a god! What do you call these things? Dreams? Jokes from the unknown wanderer? Blasphemies that cry out for the gibbet? Wait! By God, here is another marvel! Don't I see, dressed up in motley fawn-skins, the prophet Tiresias? And my mother's father here too — O depth of scorn! — adoring with the wand of Bacchus? Father! No — my eyes deceive me; it is not your white heads so caught up in this fancy! It cannot be! Cast off that ivy crown, O father of my own mother! Set free that hand cowering around its staff. — You planned this work, Tiresias! You! You must set up another altar and yet another among us, watch new birds, and earn more pay of gold by interpreting fresh signs of fire! If your hair were not silver, I tell you the truth, you would now be sitting chained in the middle of your raving women, for this evil dream you have brought us — these new gods! Once the gleam of grapes lights up a Women's Festival, there is no more soundness in their prayers at all! [LEADER OF THE CHORUS — the words are not heard by PENTHEUS.] Outrageous king, have you no fear of God, no respect for Cadmus, who sowed the Giants' Sod, life-spring of great Echion and of you?

TIRESIAS. Good words come easily, my son, when the speaker is wise and speaks for what is right. Otherwise they never come at all! Yours are swift and bright, as if with thought, but they have no thought in them at all. Look — this new God, whom you flout, I cannot tell you the greatness with which He shall be great in Hellas! Two spirits, young Prince, are first in worth among men. One is named Demeter — the Earth, call her by what name you will — who feeds the body of man with the sustenance of dry things. The other, who came after, to perfect her work, is the Power born from Semele. He found the liquid shower hidden in the grape. He gives rest to man's troubled spirit when the vine exalts him. He gives sleep, to drown the day's frets in cool forgetting. Is there any cure for man's sore heart but to forget? Yes — being God himself, his blood is poured in sacrifice before the gods, that for his sake we may be blessed. — And so, this fable shames him in your eyes, this story of how the god was knit into the flesh of God? Then learn the truth, cleared of falsehood. When Zeus rescued the babe from that deadly flame and lifted him to Olympus' height, and Hera in her wrath would have cast him from there, then Zeus devised a divine defense. He tore off a fragment of the world-encircling fire, shaped it as he wished into the image of the child, and gave that to Hera's rage. So, beguiled by change and the passage of time, this story was born — that the babe-god was hidden in the torn flesh of his sire. He has nothing to be ashamed of in it. He is a prophet, too. Prophecy clings to all frenzy, but above all to the frenzy of prayer. Then the God himself dwells in us, truly, and speaks the thing to come. He has a share of Ares' realm as well: when armies, mailed and arrayed, are seized with strange fear before blade meets blade and flee in madness, it is this God who has palsied them. Yes — over the rock-built diadem of Delphi you shall yet see him leaping with his train of fire across the twin-peaked mountain plain, flaming the darkness with his mystic wand, great in Hellas. — Listen and understand, King Pentheus! Do not dream that force is power; nor, if you have a thought, and that thought soured and sickly, do not dream that thought is wisdom! Up, receive this God to Thebes; pour out the cup of sacrifice, and pray, and wreathe your brow. You fear for the women? Think it through: how does it concern Dionysus to keep women chaste against their will? It lies with them, and with their own hearts; and in the wildest of rites no stain comes to her whose heart is white. Listen — you take joy when the Gate is thronged with people and Pentheus' name is lifted up, great and high, by Thebes in clamor; shall He not also rejoice in his rightful share of majesty? At any rate, this Cadmus you scorn, and I, will wear his crown and tread his dances! Yes — our hair is white, but this dance shall still be danced! I will not lift my arm to make war on God for you, no matter what you say. Madness most terrible is on you — madness wrought by some dread spell, but no spell or doctor's craft can cure it!
CHORUS. Gray prophet, your word is worthy of Phoebus, and wise in honoring Bromius, our great God.

CADMUS. My son, Tiresias points your road well. Make your home here with us, not standing alone against custom. This quick bird-like beating of your thought where no thought lives — that is hazardous. Grant that this God is nothing — yet let that Nothing be Something on your lips. Lie boldly, and say He IS! Then north and south will marvel that a divine thing sprang from Semele's flesh, and our whole line will be honored.

[Drawing nearer to PENTHEUS.] Is there not blood before your eyes even now? Our lost Actaeon's blood, whom long ago his own red hounds tore to death through that dim forest yonder, because he boasted himself against most holy Artemis? Beware! Let me wreathe your temples. Make your prayer with us, and walk humbly in God's sight.
[He makes as if to set the wreath on PENTHEUS' head.] PENTHEUS. Down with that hand! Be off with you to your rite, and don't smear your foul contagion on me!

[Turning upon TIRESIAS.] This man — the head and prompter of your folly — shall not miss the justice he needs! Go, half my guard — out to the rock-seat where he sits enthroned over birds and omens; rip the stone open with crowbar and trident, make one wreck of high and low, and toss his ribbons to all the winds of the air! Ha — have I found a way to sting you there? The rest of you, out through the town! Find this girl-faced stranger, who has done such damage to all Thebes, preying on our girls and wives. Search till you find him; bring him here in chains, until he is judged and stoned, and weeps in blood the day he troubled Pentheus with his god!

[The guards set forth in two bodies; PENTHEUS goes into the Castle.] TIRESIAS. Hard-hearted man, how little you know what seed you are sowing! Blind before, and now indeed most mad! — Come, Cadmus, let us go our way, and pray for this our persecutor, and pray for this poor city, that the righteous God not move in anger. — Take your ivy rod, and help my steps as I help yours. It would be a bad thing if two old men should fall on the road. Still — come what may, our service shall be done to Bacchus, the All-Father's mystic son. O Pentheus, named of sorrow! Will he claim from all your house the fulfillment of his name, old Cadmus? — No, I do not speak from my prophet's art, but from what I see — blind words and a blind heart!
[The two old men go off toward the Mountain.]

chapters.title: First Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. You Immaculate on high; you Recording Purity; you who stoop with golden wings, earthward, manward, in pity — do you hear this angry King? Do you hear the rage and scorn against the Lord of Many Voices, the one of mortal mother born, the one in whom the human heart rejoices, girt with garlands and with glee, first in Heaven's sovereignty? For his kingdom is there — in the dancing and the prayer, in the music and the laughter, in the vanishing of care, in the before and after; in the gods' high banquet, when the grape-blood gleams and flashes up to heaven; yes, and in the feasts of men comes his crowned slumber, when pain is dead and hate forgiven!

CHORUS. Loose your lips from the rein; lift your wisdom up into disdain; whatever law you cannot see, scorn it — and the end shall be calamity to the uttermost! It is the life of quiet breath, the simple and the true, that no storm or earthquake can shatter; nothing can undo the house where they live. For, far away, hidden from the eyes of day, watchers stand in the skies, who see man's life and prize the deeds well done by things of clay. But the world's Wise are not wise, claiming more than mortals may. Life is such a little thing — look, their present is already gone, and the dreams they cling to do not come. Mad imaginings are theirs, I think, and empty hearts!

CHORUS. Where is the Home for me? O Cyprus, set in the sea, Aphrodite's home in the soft sea-foam — would I could go to you, where the wings of the Loves are folded and the heart of the world grows faint. To Paphos' island, where the rainless meadows smile, with riches rolled from the hundredfold mouths of the far-off Nile, streaming beneath the waves to the roots of the seaward caves. But there is a better land, where Olympus cleaves the air, the high still dell where the Muses dwell, fairest of all things fair! There is Grace, and there is the Heart's Desire, and peace to adore you, you Spirit of Guiding Fire! * * * * * He is a God of Heaven, and born in majesty; yet he has joy in the joys of the Earth, and he loves the one who brings increase, the Feeder of Children, Peace. He bears no grudge against the great; he has no scorn for the lowly; but to all who live he gives his wine, griefless, immaculate; only on those who spurn Joy may his anger burn. Love the Day and the Night; be glad of the Dark and the Light; and turn your eyes away from the lore of the wise, who win honor in the eyes of proud men. The simple nameless herd of Humanity has deeds and faith that are truth enough for me!
[As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading in the

chapters.title: Second Episode
paragraphs: [As the Chorus ceases, a party of the guards return, leading DIONYSUS in their midst, bound. The SOLDIER in command stands forth, as PENTHEUS, hearing the tramp of feet, comes out from the Castle.]

SOLDIER. Our quest is finished, O King, and your prey is caught; for the chase was swift, and this wild thing most tame. Yet he never flinched, never thought of flight, but held both hands out without resistance — no change of color, no blanching of the wine-red cheek. He waited while we came, and bade us carry out all your decree; yes, he laughed, and made my task easy, until for very shame I confessed and said: "O stranger, it is not by my own will that I bind you, but to fulfill the bidding of the one who sent me." And those imprisoned women you seized and bound within the wall of your great dungeon — they are gone, O King, free in the woods, dancing and glorying in Bromius. Of their own accord, they say, the fetters fell from them and the manacles, and the bars slid back untouched by mortal hand. Yes — full of many wonders is this man come to your land. Yet still it lies with you!
PENTHEUS. You are mad! — Untie him. However swift he is, my snares are around him and he shall not get away.

[The guards loose the arms of DIONYSUS; PENTHEUS studies him for a while in silence, then speaks jeeringly. DIONYSUS remains gentle and unafraid.] Well, well — a fair shape for a woman's eye, sir stranger! And I bet that is exactly what you are after! Long curls too — that shows you have never been a wrestler! — falling so softly down both cheeks, charming. And a white skin! It must have cost you pains to please your women with this white-and-red of cheeks that never see the sunlight!
[DIONYSUS is silent.] Speak, fellow; tell me your name and your race first.
DIONYSUS. There is no glory in it, nor any disgrace. You have heard of Tmolus, the bright hill of flowers?
PENTHEUS. Of course; the ridge that winds past Sardis' towers.
DIONYSUS. From there I come; Lydia was my fatherland.
PENTHEUS. And these revelations your band is spreading through Hellas — where do they come from?
DIONYSUS. Their meaning and use Dionysus disclosed to me, the Child of Zeus. PENTHEUS (brutally). Is there a Zeus there, who can still beget young gods?
DIONYSUS. No — only the Zeus whose seal was set on Semele here in your Thebes.
PENTHEUS. In what way did he come down upon you? In broad daylight, or in a vision of the night?
DIONYSUS. He stood before me clearly, and looked into my soul, and gave his emblems into my hand.
PENTHEUS. What sort of things are they, these emblems?
DIONYSUS. That none may reveal nor know, except his Elect alone.
PENTHEUS. And what good do they bring to the worshipper?
DIONYSUS. A good beyond price — but not for you to hear.
PENTHEUS. Trickster! You're trying to provoke me to seek them out!
DIONYSUS. His mysteries abhor the touch of sinners.
PENTHEUS. So your eyes saw this God plainly; what shape did he have?
DIONYSUS. Whatever shape pleased him. It was not for me to ordain his form.
PENTHEUS. There again — deftly turned aside. An idle joke, and nothing answered!
DIONYSUS. To blinded eyes, wise words seem like nothing.
PENTHEUS. And have you come to Thebes first, to have your god established?
DIONYSUS. No — all the lands of the Barbarians have danced his dance before this.
PENTHEUS. A low, blind people, I think, beside our Hellenes!
DIONYSUS. Higher and keener in this, though their ways are not your way.
PENTHEUS. Is your worship held by night or by day?
DIONYSUS. Most often by night; the darkness is a majestic thing.
PENTHEUS. Ha! With women worshipping? It is a craft and a rottenness!
DIONYSUS. By day, no less, anyone who looks for it can find unholiness.
PENTHEUS. Enough! Your sentence is fixed, for false pretense corrupting Thebes.
DIONYSUS. Not mine — but yours, for your dense blindness of heart and your blasphemy against God!
PENTHEUS. A ready knave, this mystery-priest, and brazen-faced!
DIONYSUS. Come, tell me what it shall be — my sentence; what dire thing will you do to me?
PENTHEUS. First, shear off that delicate curl that dangles there.
[He beckons to the soldiers, who approach DIONYSUS.] DIONYSUS. I have vowed it to my God; this is holy hair.
[The soldiers cut off the tress.] PENTHEUS. Next, hand me your staff!
DIONYSUS. Lift your own hand and take it. This is Dionysus' wand.
[PENTHEUS takes the staff.] PENTHEUS. Last of all, I will hold you here as a prisoner.
DIONYSUS. My Lord God will release me, when I speak the word.
PENTHEUS. He may — if ever again, in the midst of his band of saints, he hears your voice!
DIONYSUS. Even now he stands close by, and sees all that I suffer.
PENTHEUS. What? Where is he? My eyes do not see him.
DIONYSUS. Where I am! Your own impurity is what veils him from you.
PENTHEUS. The dog jeers at me! At me and at Thebes! Bind him!
[The soldiers begin to bind him.] DIONYSUS. I charge you, do not bind me! I have sight, and you are blind!
PENTHEUS. And I, with better right, say bind him all the more!

[The soldiers obey.] DIONYSUS. You do not know what end you are seeking, nor what deed you are doing, nor what man you are! PENTHEUS (mocking). Agave's son, and on the father's side Echion's, called Pentheus!
DIONYSUS. So be it — a name foretold for calamity!

PENTHEUS. Away with him; tie him up where the horses are tied. Yes — let him lie in the manger! There he can stay, staring into the darkness! And this rabble of women that clusters around you, your priestesses of worship, are my slaves now! Maybe I will sell them across the seas, here and there; or else they shall be set to work at my distaffs, to forget their timbrel and their songs of dawn!

DIONYSUS. I go; for I cannot suffer what is not permitted! But for this sin of yours — look — He whom you deny is coming after you for recompense. Yes — in your wrong against us, you have cast Him into your prison-house!
[DIONYSUS, without his wand, his hair shorn, his arms tightly bound, is led off by the guards to his dungeon. PENTHEUS returns into the Palace.]

chapters.title: Second Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. Achelous' roaming daughter, holy Dirce, virgin water — did he not bathe in you of old, the Babe of God, the Mystery? When out of the immortal fire to himself his God did take him, into his own flesh, and spoke to him: "Enter now life's second portal, motherless Mystery; behold, I break my own body for your sake, you of the Twofold Door, and seal you mine, O Bromius" — so he spoke — "and to this your land reveal you."

CHORUS. Still my prayer trembles toward you, Dirce, still to you I hurry. Why, O Blessed among Rivers, do you fly from me and deny me? By his own joy I swear, by the grape upon the bough, you shall seek Him in the midnight, you shall love Him, even now!

CHORUS. Dark, and impassioned with the dark, is this Pentheus' blood; yes, he is fashioned out of the Dragon, born from Echion, child of Earth. He is no man, but a wonder; did the Earth-Child not beget him as a red Giant, to set him up against God, against the Thunder? He will bind me as his prize — me, the Bride of Dionysus; and my priest, my friend, has been taken — even now lies buried; in the dark he lies forsaken!

CHORUS. Look — we run a race with death; we are perishing, Dionysus, here before you! Do you not mark us, do you not cherish those who implore you and adore you? Hither down Olympus' side, come, O Holy One defied — let your golden wand be lifted over the tyrant in his pride!

CHORUS. Where are you? In your own Nysa, you our only help? Are you waving your thronging thyrsus over fierce beasts in eastern lands, by the high Corycian Cave, or where stern Olympus stands? In the elm-woods and the oaken, there where Orpheus harped of old, when the trees awoke and knew him, and the wild things gathered to him, as he sang amid the broken glens his music manifold? Blessed Land of Pieria, Dionysus loves you; he will come to you with dancing, come with joy and mystery; with the Maenads at his bidding winding, winding to the West; crossing the flood of swiftly glancing Axios in majesty; crossing the Lydias, the giver of good gifts and waving green; crossing that Father-Stream of story, rolling through a land of horses and of glory — bravest, fairest river ever seen by mortals!
THE VOICE. Io! Io! Awake, you women; hear my cry, calling my Chosen — listen, all of you!
CHORUS. Who speaks? What echo is this?
CHORUS. A Voice — a Voice that calls us!
THE VOICE. Be of good cheer! Look — it is I, the Child of Zeus and Semele.
CHORUS. O Master, Master — it is You!
CHORUS. O Holy Voice, be with us now!
THE VOICE. Spirit of the Chained Earthquake, hear my word! Awake, awake!
[An Earthquake suddenly shakes the pillars of the Castle.] CHORUS. Ah! What is coming? Shall the hall of Pentheus be racked and fall in ruin?
LEADER. Our God is in the house! Maidens, adore Him!
CHORUS. We adore Him, every one!
THE VOICE. Unveil the Lightning's eye! Wake up the fire that sleeps, against this house!

[Fire leaps up on the Tomb of Semele.] CHORUS. Ah, did you see, did you mark the flame from Semele's hallowed sod awakened? Yes — the Death that came ablaze from heaven of old, the same hot splendor of the shaft of God?

LEADER. Cast yourselves down, cast yourselves to the earth! The Lord is coming against this house! Cast yourselves down, you trembling girls; He, our adored, the Child of God, has come, and all is overthrown!
[The Maidens cast themselves upon the ground, eyes lowered. DIONYSUS, alone and unbound, enters from the Castle.]

chapters.title: Third Episode
paragraphs: DIONYSUS. You Damsels of the Morning Hills, why are you lying there dismayed? You marked, did you, our Master, and the mighty hand he laid on tower and rock, shaking the house of Pentheus? — But arise, cast the trembling from your flesh, and lift untroubled eyes.
LEADER. O Light in Darkness, is it you? O Priest, is this your face? My heart leaps out to greet you from the depth of loneliness.
DIONYSUS. Did you despair so quickly when I passed beneath the Gate? Did you think the gates of Pentheus could quell me, or his darkness hold me fast?
LEADER. Oh, what was left if you were gone? What could I do but despair? How did you escape that man of sin? Who freed you from the snare?
DIONYSUS. I had no pain, no peril; my own hand set me free.
LEADER. But your arms were chained!

DIONYSUS. No — no chain, no touch, was laid on me! That is exactly where I mocked him, in his chains, and gave him dreams to feed on. For when he led me down, behold, before the stall there stood a Bull of Offering. And this King — he bit his lips, and straight away fell on it and bound it, hoof and limb, gasping with wrath and sweat. And I sat there watching! Then a Voice — and lo, our Lord had come, and the house shook, and a great flame stood over his mother's tomb. And Pentheus rushed this way and that, calling his slaves for water, lest his roof-tree burn — and they all toiled, all in vain. Then suddenly he thought I had gone; he abandoned the fire, and sped back to the prison gates, his lifted sword shining red. But there, I think, the God had wrought — I speak only as I guess — some dream-shape in my likeness; for he stabbed at empty air, struggled in fury, as if it were me he was killing. Then in the midst of his dreams God struck him yet again! He brought down all that high house. And there in wreckage forevermore it lies, that the day of my bondage may be sore in Pentheus' eyes! And now his sword is fallen, and he lies worn out and pale — he who dared, mortal that he was, to rise in wrath against his God. And I rose up and left him, and in all peace took my path out to my Chosen, caring little for Pentheus and his anger. But quiet — I think a footstep sounds even now within the hall; here he is. How will he stand, do you think, and what will he say? I will bear with him gently, even if he comes in burning fury. The ways of Wisdom are still, and her temper does not tremble.

[Enter PENTHEUS in fury.] PENTHEUS. It is too much! This Eastern knave has slipped his prison, whom I just now held hard gripped in chains. — Ha! It is he! — What, sir, how do you show yourself before my doors?
[He advances furiously upon him.] DIONYSUS. Softly, you! Set a quiet bearing on your rage.
PENTHEUS. How did you get out here? How did you break your cage? Speak!
DIONYSUS. Did I not tell you — or did you fail to mark it — there was One living who would set me free?
PENTHEUS. Who? These tales of yours grow wilder and wilder.
DIONYSUS. He who first made the clustered vine for man.
PENTHEUS. I scorn him and his vines!
DIONYSUS. For Dionysus, that is well; for in your scorn his glory lies. PENTHEUS (to his guard). Hurry to all the towers, and bar every gate as well!
DIONYSUS. What — can a god not leap a wall?
PENTHEUS. Oh, you have wit — except where you need it!
DIONYSUS. Wherever it most matters, there my wit is! — Quiet! Wait until the man who hurries here from the mountainside with news for you arrives. We will not flee, but wait on your command.
[Enter suddenly and in haste a Messenger from the Mountain.] MESSENGER. Great Pentheus, Lord of all this Theban land, I come from high Cithaeron, where the frosty snow gleams and never ceases. . .
PENTHEUS. And what news of importance does your coming bring?

MESSENGER. I have seen the Wild White Women there, O King, whose fleet limbs darted arrow-like just now from Thebes — and I have come to tell you how they work strange deeds, marvel beyond marvel. But first I would learn your pleasure. Shall I tell my whole tale, or veil the strangest part? I fear, my Lord, the swiftness of your heart, your edged wrath, your more-than-royal soul.
PENTHEUS. Your tale shall not harm you. — Tell it all. It is wrong to be angry with honesty. No — if your news of them is dark, it is the one who bewitched and led them on who shall pay the price.

MESSENGER. Our herds of cattle were moving up to the peaks at dawn — the grayest, coldest hour, when the first rays steal earthward and the rime begins to yield — when I saw three bands of them. Autonoe led one, Ino another, the third your own mother, Agave. There beneath the trees they lay sleeping, like wild things flung at ease in the forest; one half-sinking on a bed of deep pine greenery; one with careless head among the fallen oak leaves; all most cold in purity — not as your tale of them was told, of wine-cups and wild music and the chase for love amid the lonely forest. Then suddenly Queen Agave rose up among her band, and gave the God's wild cry: "Awake, you Bacchanals! I hear the sound of horned cattle. Awake!" — Then all around them, alert, the warm sleep falling from their eyes, I saw them rise in a marvel of swift ranks — women young and old, gentle unwed maidens among them. Over their shoulders first they shook their hair, and gathered up the fallen folds of mantles where some clasp had loosened, and girt the dappled fawn-skins to their bodies with long quick snakes that hissed and writhed with quivering tongues. One held a young fawn, another a wolf cub, and fed them with white milk, and smiled in love — young mothers with a mother's breast, their own babes at home forgotten! Then they pressed wreaths of ivy and oak sprays and flowering bryony around their brows. One would lift her wand and strike the rock, and at once a jet of quick bright water came. Another set her thyrsus in the bosomed earth, and there a darkling fountain of red wine sprang up, sent up by the God for her. And if any lips wanted whiter draughts, with dipping fingertips they pressed the sod, and gushing from the ground came springs of milk. And the reed-wands wreathed in ivy ran with sweet honey, drop by drop. — O King, if you had been there as I was, and seen this thing, with prayer and most high wonder you would have gone to adore this God whom now you rail upon! Anyway, the cattle-keepers and shepherds came together in one place, amazed, and held a council; and one being there who walked the streets and knew the ways of speech took the lead among them — those whose hands knew only the slow soil and the solemn hill — and spoke flatteringly, and asked: "Masters, is it your will that we stop the king's mother, Agave, from her lawless worship, and win some royal thanks?" — And this seemed good to all; and through the branching underwood we hid ourselves, cowering in the leaves. There for the appointed hour they made their prayer and worshipped the Wand, with one accord of heart and cry — "Iacchus, Bromius, Lord, God of God born!" — And all the mountain felt it, and worshipped with them; and the wild things knelt and reared and gloried, and the wilderness was filled with moving voices and dim straining sound. Soon, as it happened, the Queen herself passed dancing close by my thicket, and I rose and sprang to seize her. But she turned her face on me and cried: "Ho, my rovers of the chase, my wild White Hounds — we are hunted! Up, every staff of you, and follow, follow, for our Lord and our God!" Thereupon, in fear that they would tear us apart, we all fled, amazed; and on, with empty hands, they swept toward our herds that browsed the green hill-grass. Then you would have seen great-uddered cattle bellowing in sword-like hands that cleaved and tore — a living steer ripped asunder, the air tossed with rent ribs and limbs of cloven hoof, flesh hanging on the branches, and red rain dripping down the deep green pines. Yes — proud bulls, horns swift to rage, were fronted and flung stumbling sideways by those many hands and dragged down without pity. The bands of clothed flesh and bone were unbound from each other faster than the lids could fall on your royal eyes. Then on like birds, borne up by their own speed, they swept toward the plains of waving corn that lie beside Asopus' banks and bring to Thebes the rich harvest of her fields. On Hysiae and Erythrae, that lie nursed amid the bowering rocks of Cithaeron, they burst, destroying like an enemy's army. They snatched up little children from their homes high on their shoulders — babes unheld, who swayed and laughed and did not fall. They wrecked everything; bronze and iron they shattered, and tossed about in play, and yet not one of them took a wound; they caught fire from the hearths, and carried hot flames in their hair — and were not scorched! The villagers in wrath took up spear and sword, and turned upon the Bacchae. Then, dread Lord, was the wonder. Spear and barbed blade could not scathe nor touch the women; but the wand — the soft and wreathed wand that their white hands sped — blasted those men and quelled them, and they fled dizzily. Some God surely was in these things! And the holy women returned to those strange springs that God had sent them when the day dawned on the upper heights, and washed away the stain of battle. And those girdling snakes hissed out and lapped the waterdrops from cheek and hair and breast. So I counsel you, O King — receive this Spirit, whoever he is, into Thebes in glory. Greatness manifold is all about him; and the tale is told that this is he who first gave to man the grief-assuaging vine. Oh, let him live; for if he dies, then Love herself is slain, and nothing joyful is left in the world!
LEADER. Though I tremble, and scarcely dare speak my thought to a king's face, yet I will not hide it. Dionysus is God, and no God truer or higher!

PENTHEUS. It bursts close at hand, like a smoldering fire, this frenzy of Bacchic women! All my land is made their mockery. — This calls for an iron hand! Captain! Quick, to the Electran Gate! Order all my men-at-arms to gather there; call out everyone who can spur a horse, every man who can wield the round shield or bend the bow; we march to war! — By God, shall women dare such deeds against us? It is too much to bear!

DIONYSUS. You do not heed me, O King, and you make light of my solemn words; yet, in spite of yourself, I warn you still. Do not lift your spear against a god — hold your peace, and fear his wrath! He will not stand it, if you frighten his Chosen out of the hills of their delight.
PENTHEUS. Quiet, you! And if for once you have slipped your chain, give thanks for it! — Or shall I knot your arms again?
DIONYSUS. Better to give him prayer and sacrifice than kick against the goads, since Dionysus is God, and you only mortal.
PENTHEUS. That I will give him! Yes — sacrifice of women's blood, to call his name through all of Cithaeron!
DIONYSUS. You shall all flee, and lower your bronze-rimmed shields before their wands.
PENTHEUS. There is no way with this man — this stranger that dogs us! Whether I treat him well or ill, he must keep babbling!
DIONYSUS. Wait, my friend! These crooked matters may yet be straightened out.
[PENTHEUS has started as though to seek his army at the gate.] PENTHEUS. Yes — by obeying my own slaves' will. How else?
DIONYSUS. I myself will lead the women here, without sword or horse.
PENTHEUS. What now? — This is some plot against me!
DIONYSUS. What do you fear? It is only to save you that I plot.
PENTHEUS. It is some compact you have made, you and they, to dance these hills forever!

DIONYSUS. Truly, that is my compact, sworn with my Lord! PENTHEUS (turning from him). Ho, armorers! Bring out my shield and sword! — And you, be silent! DIONYSUS (after regarding him fixedly, speaks with resignation). Ah! — Have your way, then!

[He fixes his eyes upon PENTHEUS again, while the armorers bring out his armor; then speaks in a tone of command.] Man, you would gladly look on them at their prayers on the mountain! PENTHEUS (who during the rest of this scene, with a few exceptions, simply speaks the thoughts that DIONYSUS puts into him, losing power over his own mind). That I would — though it cost me all the gold of Thebes!
DIONYSUS. So much? You are quick to fall into such great longing. PENTHEUS (somewhat bewildered by what he has said). Yes — it would grieve me much to see them flown with wine.
DIONYSUS. And yet you crave a sight that would much grieve you?
PENTHEUS. Yes; I would gladly watch, hidden among the pines.
DIONYSUS. It would be vain to hide. They would soon track you out.
PENTHEUS. Well said! Best to do it openly.
DIONYSUS. Will you be led by me, and try the venture?
PENTHEUS. Yes, indeed! Lead on. Why should we delay?
DIONYSUS. First we need a rich and trailing robe of fine linen to cover you.
PENTHEUS. What — am I a woman, then, and no longer a man?
DIONYSUS. Would you have them kill you outright? No man may see their mysteries.
PENTHEUS. Well said! — I marked your subtle temper long ago.
DIONYSUS. It is Dionysus that prompts me.
PENTHEUS. And how do you mean to carry out the rest of the plan?
DIONYSUS. First go inside. I will dress you.
PENTHEUS. In what dress? Woman's clothing? No — I will not.
DIONYSUS. Does it change so soon, all your desire to see this strange worship?
PENTHEUS. Wait! What outfit will you put on me?
DIONYSUS. First, a long lock dangling low beneath your shoulders.
PENTHEUS. Yes — and next?
DIONYSUS. The robe I mentioned, falling to your feet; and on your head a snood.
PENTHEUS. And after that? Have you anything more?
DIONYSUS. Of course; the dappled fawn-skin and the wand. PENTHEUS (after a struggle with himself). Enough! I cannot wear a robe and a snood.
DIONYSUS. Would you rather draw the sword and spill men's blood? PENTHEUS (again doubting). True, that would be evil. — Yes; better to go first to some place to watch from.
DIONYSUS. Far wiser, than to seek wrath's bitter recompense by wrath.
PENTHEUS. What of the city streets? Can you lead me out unseen by anyone?
DIONYSUS. Lonely and untried your path from here shall be, and I your guide!
PENTHEUS. I care for nothing, so long as these Bacchanals do not triumph over me! . . . Forward into my halls within! — I will decide what seems best.

DIONYSUS. So be it, O King! It is mine to obey your command, whatever it is. PENTHEUS (after hesitating once more and waiting). Well, I will go — perhaps to march and scatter them with serried lance, perhaps to take your plan. . . . I do not know yet.

[Exit PENTHEUS into the Castle.] DIONYSUS. Maidens, the lion walks into the net! He finds his Bacchae now, and sees, and dies, and pays for all his sin! — O Dionysus, this is your hour, and you not far away. Grant us our vengeance! — First, O Master, halt the course of reason in him, and instill in him a foam of madness. Let his seeing will, which would never have stooped to put on your vesture, be darkened, until the deed is lightly done. Grant likewise that he find through all his streets loud scorn, this man of wrath and bitter threats who made Thebes tremble — led now in woman's guise. I go to fold that robe of sacrifice on Pentheus, the robe that shall deck him for the dark — his mother's gift! — So shall he learn and mark God's true Son, Dionysus, fully God, most fearful, yet to man most soft of mood.
[Exit DIONYSUS, following PENTHEUS into the Castle.]

chapters.title: Third Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. Will they ever come to me, ever again, the long, long dances? On through the dark till the dim stars wane? Shall I feel the dew on my throat, the stream of wind in my hair? Shall our white feet gleam in the dim expanses? O feet of a fawn fled to the greenwood, alone in the grass and the loveliness — leap of the hunted, no more in dread, beyond the snares and the deadly press: yet a voice still in the distance sounds, a voice and a fear and a haste of hounds; O wildly laboring, fiercely fleet, onward and onward by river and glen . . . Is it joy or terror, you storm-swift feet? . . . To the dear lone lands untroubled by men, where no voice sounds, and amid the shadowy green the little things of the woodland live unseen. What else is Wisdom? What can man's striving, or God's high grace, be more lovely or more great? To stand free of fear, to breathe and wait; to hold a hand uplifted over Hate; and shall not Loveliness be loved forever?

CHORUS. O Strength of God, slow are you and still, yet you never fail! On those who worship the Ruthless Will, on those who dream, your judgment waits. The dreams of the proud, making things great and ever greater, things that are not of God. In wide and devious coverts, hunter-wise, He couches himself with Time's unhurried stride, following, following, the man whose eyes do not look up to Heaven. For all is vain — the pulse of the heart, the plot of the brain, that strives beyond the laws that live. And is your Faith so much to give? Is it so hard a thing to see, that the Spirit of God, whatever it may be, the Law that abides and does not change, ages long, the Eternal and the Nature-born — these things are strong? What else is Wisdom? What can man's striving, or God's high grace, be more lovely or more great? To stand free of fear, to breathe and wait; to hold a hand uplifted over Hate; and shall not Loveliness be loved forever?

LEADER. Happy the man on the weary sea who has fled the tempest and reached the haven. Happy whoever has risen, free, above his striving. For strangely graven is the orb of life — that one and another in gold and power may outpass his brother. Men in their millions float and flow, and seethe with a million hopes as leaven; and they win their Will, or they miss their Will, and their hopes either die or are pined for still. But whoever can know, as the long days go, that to LIVE is happiness — he has found his Heaven!
[Re-enter DIONYSUS from the Castle.]

chapters.title: Fourth Episode
paragraphs: DIONYSUS. O eye that craves sights you must not see, O heart athirst for what cannot slake! You, Pentheus, I call — come forth and be seen, in the guise of a woman, a Maenad, a saint of Dionysus, to spy upon his Chosen and your own mother!
[Enter PENTHEUS, dressed like a Bacchanal, strangely excited, a spirit of Bacchic madness overshadowing him.] Your shape, I think, is like one of Cadmus' royal daughters!

PENTHEUS. Yes; and my eye is bright! That sun shines double in the sky, and Thebes double, and the Wall of Seven Gates. . . . And is this a Wild Bull I see, walking and waiting before me? There are horns upon your brow! What are you, man or beast? For surely now the Bull is upon you!
DIONYSUS. He who used to be wrathful goes with us now in gentleness. He has unsealed your eyes to see what you should see.
PENTHEUS. Tell me — do I not stand as Ino stands, or as my mother does?
DIONYSUS. When I look on you, it seems I see their very selves! — But wait — why does that lock stream loose, and not where I laid it, crossed under the coif?

PENTHEUS. I did it, while I tossed my head in dancing, to and fro, and cried his holy music! DIONYSUS (tending him). I shall soon tie it right. It is mine to tend you. . . . There — but stand with your head straight.
PENTHEUS. I am in the hollow of your hand. Adorn me as you will.
DIONYSUS. Your sash is loosened too; and the folds of the gown do not fall evenly to the feet.

PENTHEUS. So it seems, on the right foot. But here, I think, they fall in one straight line to the heel. DIONYSUS (while tending him). And if you find their madness true — yes, more than true — what love and thanks will you give me? PENTHEUS (not listening to him). In my right hand should I carry the wand, or thus, to be most like to them?

DIONYSUS. Up let it swing in the right hand, in time with the right foot's spring. . . . It is good your heart is changed! PENTHEUS (more wildly). What strength is this in me! Cithaeron's slopes and all that they hold — could not my shoulders, do you think, lift the whole?
DIONYSUS. Surely you can, if you will! Your soul, once so sick, now stands as it should stand.
PENTHEUS. Shall it be bars of iron? Or this bare hand and shoulder against the crags, to wrench them down?
DIONYSUS. Would you wreck the Nymphs' wild temples, and the brown rocks where Pan pipes at noon?
PENTHEUS. No — not I! Force is not the right thing for women. I will lie hidden in the pine-thickets.

DIONYSUS. Even as suits a spy upon holy and fearful things, so shall you lie! PENTHEUS (with a laugh). They lie there even now, I think — wild birds, caught by love among the leaves, and not fluttering!
DIONYSUS. It may be. That is what you go to see — yes, and to trap them — so they don't trap you!
PENTHEUS. Forth through the Thebans' town! I am their king, yes, their one Man, since I dare to do this thing!
DIONYSUS. Yes, you alone shall bear their burden — therefore your trial awaits you! — But come on; with me into your ambush you shall come unscathed; then let another bear you home!
PENTHEUS. The Queen, my mother.
DIONYSUS. Marked of every eye.
PENTHEUS. For that I go!
DIONYSUS. You shall be borne on high!
PENTHEUS. That were like pride!
DIONYSUS. Your mother's hands shall share in carrying you.
PENTHEUS. No — I have no need of such soft care!
DIONYSUS. So soft?
PENTHEUS. Whatever it is, I have well earned it!

[Exit PENTHEUS toward the Mountain.] DIONYSUS. Fell, fell are you; and to a doom so fell you walk that your name from South to North shall shine, a sign for ever! — Reach forth your arms now, Agave, and you dark-browed sisters of Cadmus' line! Greet this proud prince to his high ordeal, where none walks unscathed except God and me! — The rest, this day shall see.
[Exit DIONYSUS, following PENTHEUS.] CHORUS.

chapters.title: Fourth Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. O hounds raging and blind, up by the mountain road, spirits of the maddened mind, on to the wild Maids of God; fill their eyes with your rage, rage at the rage unblest, the watcher in woman's guise, the spy on God's Possessed.

CHORUS. Who shall be the first to mark him — eyes in the rock that spy, eyes in the pine-tree dark — is it his mother? — and cry: "Look, what is this that comes haunting, troubling still, even on our heights, our homes, the wild Maids of the Hill? What flesh bore this child? Never on woman's breast did changeling so evil smile; this is no man, but a Beast! Lion-shape of the wild, Gorgon-breed of the waste!"

CHORUS. Hither, for doom and deed! Hither with lifted sword, Justice, Wrath of the Lord, come in our visible need! Smite till the throat shall bleed, smite till the heart shall bleed, him the tyrannous, lawless, godless, Echion's earth-born seed!

CHORUS. Tyrannously has he trodden; he has marched, in defiance of Law, against your Light, O God, yes, and against your Mother's Light; he has girded himself, falsely bold, blinded in his own craft, to crush by man's violence things unconquerable.

CHORUS. A strait, pitiless mind is death to godliness; and to feel oneself one with mankind is life, and a pain the less. Knowledge, we are not enemies! I seek you diligently; but the world with a great wind blows, shining, and not from you; blowing toward beautiful things, on, amid dark and light, until Life, through the trammels of Laws that are not the Right, breaks, clean and pure, and sings glory to God in the height!

CHORUS. Hither, for doom and deed! Hither with lifted sword, Justice, Wrath of the Lord, come in our visible need! Smite till the throat shall bleed, smite till the heart shall bleed, him the tyrannous, lawless, godless, Echion's earth-born seed!

LEADER. Appear, appear, whatever your shape or your name — O Mountain Bull, Snake of the Hundred Heads, Lion of Burning Flame! O God, Beast, Mystery, come! Your mystic maids are hunted! — Blast their hunter with your breath, cast over his head your snare; and laugh aloud and drag him to his death, who stalks your herded madness in its lair!
[Enter hastily a MESSENGER from the Mountain, pale and distraught.]

chapters.title: Exodos
paragraphs: [Enter hastily a MESSENGER from the Mountain, pale and distraught.] MESSENGER. Woe to the house once blessed in Hellas! Woe to you, old Sidonian King, who sowed the dragon-seed on Ares' bloody field! Even your slaves must weep for you!
LEADER. News from the mountain? — Speak! How has it gone?
MESSENGER. Pentheus, my king, son of Echion, is dead!
LEADER. All hail, God of the Voice, Manifest evermore!
MESSENGER. What are you saying? — How strange your tone, as though you rejoiced at this overthrow of my master!
LEADER. With fierce joy I rejoice, child of a savage shore; for the chains of my prison are broken, and the dread in which I cowered before!
MESSENGER. And do you think Thebes so destitute, so empty of manhood, that it must sit beneath your scorn?
LEADER. Thebes has no power over me! No one but Him do I obey, Dionysus, Child of the Highest — Him I obey and adore!
MESSENGER. One can forgive you! — Yet it is no fair thing, women, to rejoice in a man's suffering.
LEADER. Speak of the mountainside! Tell us of the doom in which he died, the sinner struck to death, even in the very place of his sin!

MESSENGER. We climbed beyond the highest dwellings of the Theban shepherds, passed the springs of Asopus, and struck into the rocky country on dim Cithaeron — Pentheus, and, attending him, I and the Stranger who was to guide our way. First we stopped in a green dell and lay down, lips dumb and feet still, watching warily, to be unseen and yet to see. It was a narrow glen, towered over by crags, torn through by tossing waters, with a shadow of great pines lowering over it. There the Maenad maidens sat, busy in their work, busily glad. Some with an ivy chain were trailing a worn wand to make its locks toss again; some, wild in joy like young horses set free, sang back-and-forth songs of mystic melody. But my poor master could not see the great band before him. "Stranger," he cried, "from where we stand my eyes cannot reach these false saints of yours. Mount we the bank, or some high-shouldered pine, and I shall see their follies clearly!" At that there came a marvel. The Stranger reached up and touched the high heavenward crown of a great pine-tree, and lower, lower, lower he urged it down to the bare floor of the forest. Round like a bending bow, or the slow wheel-rim a joiner forces into shape, so in those hands that tough mountain stem bowed slowly — strength not mortal lived in them — until it touched the earth itself. There he set the King in the branches, and slowly, lest the tree fling him in its rebound, he let the young straining tree spring back, until it towered again amid the towering sky — with Pentheus in the branches! Well I think he saw the Maenads then, and well was seen! For he was scarcely aloft when suddenly there was no Stranger any more with me, but out of Heaven a Voice — oh, what other voice could it be? — It was He that called! "Behold, O women, I bring you the man who turns to spite both me and you, who darkens my great Light. It is yours to avenge!" So spoke he, and between earth and sky there came a pillar of high flame. And silence took the air, and no leaf stirred in all the forest dell. In that vast silence you would not have heard a single wild creature's cry. They sprang to their feet — but with bewildered eyes, gazing and listening, scarcely yet hearing aright. Then came the Voice again. And when they knew their God's clear call, the royal brood of old Cadmus — up like wild pigeons startled in a wood, on flying feet they came: his mother foremost, blind Agave, with her sisters, and behind them all the wild crowd, more deeply maddened then; through the angry rocks and torrent-tossing glen they ran, until they spied him in the dark pine. Then they climbed a crag close by, and furiously some tried to stone him, others flung their wands lance-like aloft in cruel aim. But none could hit him. The height overtopped their rage, and there he clung, untouched, as if caught in a cage. And no end was found to all their striving. Then "Hither," cried Agave; "stand round and grip the stem, my Wild Ones, till we take this climbing wildcat! He shall not make a tale of God's high dances!" Then arms upon arms shone out, past counting, and closed upon the pine, and gripped; and the ground gave way, and down it reeled. And that high sitter from the crown of the green pine-top, with a shrieking cry, fell as his mind grew clear — and there hard by was horror visible. It was his mother who stood over him, first priestess of those rites of blood. He tore off the coif and flung it from his head, that she might know him and not slay him to her own misery. He touched her wild cheek, crying: "Mother, it is I, your child, your Pentheus, born to you in Echion's hall! Have mercy, Mother! Do not let it happen, that for any sin of mine you should kill your son!" But she, with foaming lips and eyes that ran like leaping fire, with thoughts no mortal should have, possessed by Bacchus utterly, did not stay and did not hear. Round his left arm she put both hands, set her foot hard against his side, and pulled . . . and the shoulder came away! — Not by strength of arm, but easily, as the God made her hand's effort light. And on the other side Ino was tearing; and the torn flesh cried; and Autonoe pressed in, and all the crowd of ravening arms. Yes, all the air was loud with groans that faded into sobbing breath, with dim shrieks, and joy, and triumphant cries of death. One bore a severed arm, another a hunter's booted foot; bare bones lay open by the rending, and swift hands red with blood tossed in sport the flesh of Pentheus dead. His body lies far apart. Some of it the cliff has, some lurks in the tangles of the woodland — no light task to find it. And, ah, the head! That his mother holds, fixed upon a wand as one might fix a lion's; and through the land, leaving her sisters in their dancing-place, she carries it on high! Yes — to these very walls her face is set, exulting in her deed of blood, calling on her Bromius, her God, her Comrade, Fellow-Render of the Prey, her All-Victorious — to whom this day she bears in triumph . . . her own broken heart! For me, after that sight, I will go away before Agave comes. — To fulfill God's laws, and have no thought beyond his will, is man's best treasure. That, I think, is also true wisdom for things of dust to cling to.
[The MESSENGER departs into the Castle.] CHORUS.

CHORUS. Weave the dance, and call praise to God! Bless the Tyrant's fall! Down is trodden Pentheus, the Dragon's Seed! Did he wear the woman's weed? Did he clasp his death indeed, did he clasp the rod?
CHORUS. Yes, the wild ivy lapped him, and the doomed Wild Bull of Sacrifice loomed before him!
CHORUS. You who scorned Bromius, praise him the more, Bacchanals, Cadmus-born! Praise with sore agony, yes, with tears! Great are the gifts he bears! Hands that a mother lifts, red with gore!
LEADER. But wait — Agave is coming! And her eyes flash fire all about her, reeling! Look — the prize is coming! All hail, O Rout of Dionysus!

[Enter from the Mountain AGAVE, mad, and to all appearances wondrously happy, carrying the head of PENTHEUS in her hand. The CHORUS MAIDENS stand horror-struck at the sight; the LEADER, also horror-struck, tries to accept it and rejoice in it as the God's deed.]
AGAVE. You from the lands of Morn!
LEADER. Do not call to me; I give praise!
AGAVE. Look — from the trunk newly shorn, hither a Mountain Thorn we bring! O Asia-born Bacchanals, bless this chase!

LEADER. I see. Yes — I see. Have I not welcomed you? AGAVE (very calmly and peacefully). He was young, in the wildwood; without nets I caught him! No — look without fear on the Lion; I have taken him!
LEADER. Where in the wildwood? Where have you brought him from?
AGAVE. Cithaeron. . . .
LEADER. Cithaeron?
AGAVE. The Mountain has slain him!
LEADER. Who came near him first?
AGAVE. I, I — I confess it! And there beside him they named me Agave the Blessed!
LEADER. Who was next of the band on him?
AGAVE. The daughters. . .
LEADER. The daughters?
AGAVE. Of Cadmus laid hand on him. But the swift hand that slaughters is mine; mine is the praise! Bless this day of days!
[The LEADER tries to speak, but cannot; AGAVE begins gently stroking the head.]
AGAVE. Gather to the feast now!
LEADER. Feast! — O misery!
AGAVE. See — it falls to his breast, curling and gently dressed, the hair of the Wild Bull's crest — the young steer of the fell!

LEADER. Most like a beast of the wild, that head, those locks defiled. AGAVE (lifting up the head, more excitedly). He woke his Mad Ones — a Chase-God, a wise God! He flung them out to seize this thing! He preys where his band preys. LEADER (brooding, with horror). In the trail of your Mad Ones, you tear your prize, God!
AGAVE. Do you praise it?
LEADER. Should I praise this?
AGAVE. Ah, soon shall the land praise!
LEADER. And Pentheus, O Mother, your child?
AGAVE. He shall cry on my name as none other shall, and bless the spoils of the Lion!
LEADER. Yes — strange is your treasure!
AGAVE. And strange was the taking!
LEADER. You are glad?
AGAVE. Beyond measure; yes, glad in the breaking of dawn upon all this land, by the prize, the prize of my hand!
LEADER. Show then to all the land, unhappy one, the trophy of this deed that you have done!

AGAVE. Ho, all you men who dwell around the citadel and shining towers of ancient Thebes! Come! Look upon this prize, this lion's spoil, that we have taken — yes, with our own toil, we, daughters of Cadmus! Not with leather-set Thessalian javelins, not with hunter's net — only white arms and the quick fall of bladed hands. Why do you make so much fuss, and boast of your armorers' machines? Look — these palms were bare that caught the angry beast, and held him, and tore the limbs of him! . . . Father! . . . Go, bring me my father! . . . And Pentheus — where is he, my son? He shall set up a ladder against this house, and into the triglyphs there nail this lion's head for me, that gloriously I bring back, having killed him — I, even I!
[She goes through the crowd toward the Castle, showing the head and looking for a place to hang it. Enter from the Mountain CADMUS, with attendants, bearing the body of PENTHEUS on a bier.]

CADMUS. On, with your awful burden. Follow me, slaves, to his house — whose body, after a long and weary search, I found at last in the dim glens of Cithaeron, torn limb from limb, and scattered through the interweaving forest growth. — Men told me of my daughters' deed when I had just returned within these walls, with gray Tiresias, from the Bacchanals. So I hurried back to the hills again, to seek my murdered grandson. There I saw plainly Actaeon's mother, Autonoe, ranging where her son had died; and Ino at her side, wandering ghastly in the pine-thickets. Agave was not there. The rumor was that she was coming swift-footed here. — Ah! It is true; a sight I can hardly bend my eyes to look upon. AGAVE (turning from the Palace and seeing him). My father, a great boast is yours this hour. You have begotten daughters high in power and brave above all mankind — yes, all brave, though none like me! I have let fall the shuttle by the loom and raised my hand to higher things — to slay wild beasts out of your land! See, I bring the prize in my arms, that nailed up above these doors it may rise to show what your daughters have done! You take it, and call a feast. Proud you are now, and highly favored, in our valor!

CADMUS. O depth of grief, how can I fathom you, or look upon you! — Poor, poor, bloodstained hand! Poor sisters! — A fair sacrifice to set before the altars of God, my daughter! Yes, and to call my fellow citizens and me to feast on it! No — let me weep for your affliction first, then for my own. All, all of us are lost — not wrongfully, yet it is hard, to be lost at the hands of one who might have loved — our Bromius, our own!

AGAVE. How crabbed and how scowling are man's eyes in old age! — I wish my son had as good a hunter's joy as I have, in my way, when with his warrior bands he goes out to attack wild beasts! — But no, his valor goes to fighting against God's will! Father, you should set him right. . . . Will no one bring him here, that my eyes may look on his, and show him this my prize?

CADMUS. Alas! If ever you can know again the truth of what you did, what pain of pain that truth shall bring! Or would it be best for you to remain darkened forever, and to think your state not misery, since you know no happiness?
AGAVE. What do you see in this to chide, or not to bless? CADMUS (after a hesitation, resolving himself). Lift your eyes to the blue dome of air above!
AGAVE. It is done. What would you have me look for there?
CADMUS. Is it the same as before, or changed in your sight?
AGAVE. More shining than before, more heavenly bright!
CADMUS. And that wild trembling — is it still in you? AGAVE (troubled). I do not know what you are saying — but my will is clearing, and some change is coming over me, I do not know how.
CADMUS. Can you listen, then, being changed, and answer me now?
AGAVE. I have forgotten something; otherwise I could.
CADMUS. What husband led you of old from my house?
AGAVE. Echion, whom men called the Child of Earth.
CADMUS. And what child was born to you in Echion's house?
AGAVE. Pentheus — bred of my love and his father's.
CADMUS. You bear in your arms a head — what head? AGAVE (beginning to tremble, and not looking at what she carries). A lion's — so they all said in the chase.
CADMUS. Turn to it now — it is no long task — and look.
AGAVE. Ah! But what is it? What am I carrying here?
CADMUS. Look once upon it full, until all is clear!
AGAVE. I see . . . most deadly pain! Oh, woe is me!
CADMUS. Does it look like a lion to you now?
AGAVE. No — it is the head — O God! — of Pentheus, this!
CADMUS. Drenched in blood before you knew him! Yes, it is his.
AGAVE. Who killed him? — How did I come to hold this thing?
CADMUS. O cruel Truth, is this your home-coming?
AGAVE. Answer! My heart hangs upon your breath!
CADMUS. It was you. — You and your sisters wrought his death.
AGAVE. In what place was it? His own house, or where?
CADMUS. There where the dogs tore Actaeon — there.
AGAVE. Why did he go to Cithaeron? What was he seeking?
CADMUS. To mock the God and your own ecstasy.
AGAVE. But how were we on the hills this day?
CADMUS. You were mad! A spirit drove the whole land that way.

AGAVE. It is Dionysus who has done it! Now I see. CADMUS (earnestly). You wronged him! You denied his godhead! AGAVE (turning from him). Show me the body of the son I love! CADMUS (leading her to the bier). Here it is, my child. The quest for it was hard.
AGAVE. Laid out in due state?
[As there is no answer, she lifts the veil of the bier and sees.] Oh, if any sin was wrought, it was mine! What part had my child in it?

CADMUS. He made himself like to you all, refusing to adore the God; who therefore brought you and this body to one ruin, wrecking all our line, and me. Yes, no son was ever mine; and now this first-fruit of your flesh, sad woman, lies foully and frightfully here, murdered! He whom the house looked up to,

[Kneeling by the body.] O Child, my daughter's child! who held my castle walls firm; who to the people was a name of fear; and no man tried to shame my gray beard if they knew that you stood by, or else swift was their reward! — And now I go forth in dishonor, an outcast — I, the great Cadmus, who sowed the seed-rows of this state of Thebes, and reaped the wonderful harvest. O my beloved, though your heart is dull in death — O still beloved, and always beloved! Never again, then, shall you lay your hand on this white beard and speak to me your "Mother's Father"; ask, "Who wrongs you? Who slights your honor or with malice stirs your heart? Speak, and I will smite the ones who wrong you!" But now — woe, woe to me and to you also; woe to your mother, and to her sisters, woe always! Whoever does not walk in dread of the gods, let him only look on this man dead!
LEADER. I weep with you. The reward sent on Pentheus by God was due; but for you . . . it is hard.
AGAVE. My father, you can see the change in me, * * * * * * * * * *

[A page or more has been torn out here from the manuscript on which all our copies of "The Bacchae" depend. It evidently contained a speech of Agave (followed presumably by some words of the Chorus), and an appearance of DIONYSUS upon a cloud. He must have pronounced judgment on the Thebans in general, and especially on the daughters of CADMUS, justified his own action, and declared his determination to establish his godhead. Where the manuscript begins again, we find him addressing CADMUS.] * * * * *

DIONYSUS. * * * * * * * * * * And tell what gifts Time bears for you, what griefs and wonders in the winding years. For you must change and become a Serpent, strange; and beside you she whom you brought of old to be your bride from Heaven afar, Harmonia, daughter of the Lord of War. Yes, and a chariot of cattle — so spoke the word of Zeus — shall carry you and your queen through many lands, lord of a wild army of eastern spears. And many towns shall they destroy beneath you, that vast horde, until they touch Apollo's dwelling, and fulfill their doom, driven back along stormy and steep roads. You only and your wife shall Ares keep, and save alive, to the Islands of the Blest. Thus speaks Dionysus, Son confessed of no man but of Zeus! — Ah, had you seen the Truth in the hour you would not, all would have been well with you, and the Child of God your friend!
AGAVE. Dionysus, we beseech you! We have sinned!
DIONYSUS. Too late! When there was time, you knew me not!
AGAVE. We confess it. Yet your hand is too hot.
DIONYSUS. You mocked me, who am God; this is your wage.
AGAVE. Should God be like a proud man in his rage?
DIONYSUS. It is as my father, Zeus, willed it long ago. AGAVE (turning from him almost with disdain). Old Man, the word is spoken; we must go.
DIONYSUS. And since you must, what is it that you wait for?

CADMUS. Child, we are come into a deadly strait, all of us — you, poor sufferer, and your two sisters, and my sad self. Far off to barbarous men I, a gray-haired wanderer, must take my road. And then the oracle, the doom of God: that I must lead a raging far-flown horde to prey on Hellas; that I must lead my own wife, Harmonia, child of Ares, both of us discorporate and turned into haunting forms, dragon and dragon-mate, against the tombs and altar-stones of Greece, with lance upon lance behind us; and not cease from toils, like other men, nor dream, nor past the foam of Acheron find my peace at last.
AGAVE. Father! And I must wander far from you!
CADMUS. O Child, why do you reach your arms to me, as the milk-white swan yearns when the old swans die?
AGAVE. Where else can I turn? I have no home.
CADMUS. I do not know; I cannot help you.
AGAVE. Farewell, O home, O ancient tower! Look — I am cast out from my chamber, and leave you for a worse lot.
CADMUS. Go forth, go forth to misery, the way Actaeon's father went!
AGAVE. Father, for you my tears are spent.
CADMUS. No, child — it is I who must weep for you; for you and for your two sisters!
AGAVE. On all this house, in bitter way, our Lord and Master, Dionysus, has poured the utter dregs of pain!
DIONYSUS. In bitter way, for bitter was the shame you did me, when Thebes did not honor my name.

AGAVE. Then lead me where my sisters are; together let our tears be shed, our ways be wandered; where no red Cithaeron waits to gaze on me; nor I gaze back; no thyrsus stem, no song, no memory in the air. Oh, let other Bacchanals be there — not I, not I, to dream of them!
[AGAVE with her group of attendants goes out on the side away from the Mountain. DIONYSUS rises upon the Cloud and disappears.]

CHORUS. There are many shapes of mystery, and many things God brings to pass past hope or fear. The end men looked for does not come, and a path is opened where no man thought. So has it fallen here. [Exeunt.]
